terms.meaning: A portable source of electrical energy with a positive and a negative terminal.
Two or more cells joined so that the positive terminal of one meets the negative terminal of the next.
The thin wire in an incandescent lamp, which gets hot and glows when current passes.
Light Emitting Diode: a lamp with no filament, whose current flows in one direction only.
A complete conducting path from one terminal of a cell to the other, through which current flows.
A simple device that completes or breaks a circuit.
A material through which electric current flows easily.
A material through which electric current cannot pass.

items.name: Terminals of a cell
items.formula: Positive: the small metal cap. Negative: the flat metal disc.
items.example: In a cell holder, the flat disc goes towards the spring.

items.name: Joining cells
items.formula: Positive terminal to negative terminal of the next cell.
items.example: In a torch, the cap of one cell touches the flat disc of the next.

items.name: Why a bulb fuses
items.formula: Its filament is broken, so the circuit is open and no current flows.
items.example: A fused bulb will not glow, even with a new cell.

items.name: Wires of an LED
items.formula: Longer wire: positive. Shorter wire: negative.
items.example: An LED with its longer wire on the battery’s positive terminal glows.

items.name: Bulb or LED: which way round?
items.formula: A bulb glows either way round. An LED glows only when positive meets positive.
items.example: Swap the wires: the bulb stays lit but the LED goes off.

items.name: Direction of current
items.formula: From the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the cell, through the circuit.
items.example: Trace it from the cell’s cap, through the lamp, back to the flat disc.

items.name: Switch positions
items.formula: ON: closed circuit, the lamp glows. OFF: an air gap makes an open circuit, the lamp is off.
items.example: A safety pin touching two drawing pins acts as a switch in the ON position.

items.name: Where a switch can go
items.example: Before or after the lamp, it still controls the lamp.

items.name: Circuit diagram
items.formula: A drawing of a circuit using standard symbols.
items.example: Cell symbol: a long thin line (positive) beside a short thick line (negative).

items.name: LED symbol
items.formula: A triangle pointing at a bar, with two small arrows pointing away.
items.example: The triangle points the way the current flows.

items.name: DC and AC
items.formula: Cells and batteries supply direct current (DC). Wall sockets supply alternating current (AC).
items.example: A torch runs on DC. A home’s wall socket gets AC from a power plant.

items.name: Conduction tester
items.formula: A cell, a lamp and two free wire ends: the lamp glows if the material between them conducts.
items.example: Touch the ends to a key and the lamp glows. Touch them to an eraser and it does not.

items.name: Examples of conductors
items.formula: All metals, pencil lead (graphite) and the human body.
items.example: Copper, aluminium foil, a steel spoon.

items.name: Examples of insulators
items.formula: Plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass, paper, wax and cork.
items.example: The plastic cover on a wire.

items.name: Metal for house wiring
items.formula: Silver, copper and gold conduct best. Copper is used because it costs less and is plentiful.
items.example: House wires are copper, not silver.

items.name: Electrical safety
items.formula: Conductors carry the current. Insulators protect us from shocks.
items.example: Never touch a switch with wet hands, and never use a wire with damaged covering.

mistakes.text: A switch is not the source of current. The cell or battery is. The switch only completes or breaks the path.
If an LED does not glow, it may not be faulty. It may simply be connected the wrong way round.
ON means a closed circuit and OFF means an open circuit. Do not swap "open" and "closed".
The human body conducts electricity. That is why a shock is dangerous.
